mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Perun ‌place ​thunder, lightning, ​oak ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Perun ‌appears ​in slavic ‌tradition ​as ​thunder, lightning, ​oak. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Thunderer, ​striker", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Perun ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Perun ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Perun ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Perun, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​thunder ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Perun** ​(*perun*) — ‌Thunder, Lightning, ‌Oak ​· Thunderer, ​striker ​— belongs ​to the ​Slavic ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Thunder, Lightning, ​Oak". The ‌name ​means "Thunderer, ​striker"[^1].

​**Perun** is ​the thunderer ​of ‌the Slavs: ​god ‌of lightning, ​storm, and ‌the ​sacred oak, ‌patron ​of warriors ‌and guarantor ​of ​oaths. His ‌name means ‌'striker.' ‌The East ​Slavic ​chronicles place ‌him first ​among ​the gods ‌of ​Kyiv, and ​folklore kept ‌his ​axe, his ‌fire, and ​his ​wrath alive ​long ​after the ‌idols sank ‌in ​the Dnieper.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling ‌**Perun** and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/perun/). ​The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*perun* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this name; ​**Perun** ​is ​a ‌scholarly transliteration ​of ​the ‌reconstructed spoken ​form. ‌Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"Thunderer, ​striker"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Perun** ‌matches ​the conventional ‌scholarly ​romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*perun* ‌contains the ​same ​letters, ‌so no ‌lost ‌diacritics ​or ​encoding transition ‌is ​claimed. ​The editorial ‌work ​is ​to ‌fix one ​reviewed ‌reference ​spelling, ​preserve capitalization ​and ​provenance, ‌and keep ‌the ​original ‌evidence ​visible. meditation.body: Perun ​is the ‌god of ‌the strike ​— the ​moment when ​the sky ​asserts itself ​against the ‌earth and ​the ​forest smells ‌of split ​wood. Everything ‌about him ​is vertical: ‌the bolt ​falls, the ​oak points ​up, the ​oath ​rises to ‌the witness ​who will ‌enforce it. ​He is ‌violent, but ​his violence ‌is legal: ​he ‌does not ​rage, he ​**executes**. That ‌is why ‌treaties trusted ‌him and ​why rebels ​in 1071 ‌invoked him ​against ​hoarding governors; ‌he is ​the enforcer ​of an ‌order older ​than any ‌prince. To ​study Perun ​is to ​watch ​a society ‌argue with ‌its own ​thunder. The ‌chroniclers beat ​his idol ​with sticks ‌and threw ‌it in ‌the ‌river, then ​preserved his ‌name more ​carefully than ​any priest ​had — ‌in oath-texts, ​in curses, ​in ​the weeping ‌of the ​baptized. A ​god whose ​worshippers cry ‌when he ​leaves has ‌not been ​defeated; he ‌has ​been internalized. ‌Perun endures ‌as the ​sound above ​the roof ​that still ​makes everyone, ‌believer or ‌not, look ​up.[^1]
